evidence.label: Guardian aggregate and method
evidence.text: The Guardian reports 387 print stories across UK national newspapers and 99 Sun stories mentioning Flack. Inclusion was her name in headline or body during 14 Aug 2019–14 Feb 2020. Three journalists classified tone; the article says the analysis is not definitive. Most stories were neutral overall; December negative headlines rose to 35% versus 18% positive, while February had equal positive and negative counts.

evidence.label: Charge report, 13 December 2019
evidence.text: ITV reported that Flack was charged with assault by beating on 13 December after an incident the previous day. The allegation was not a conviction.

evidence.label: Flack steps down from Love Island, 17 December 2019
evidence.text: ITV reported that Flack stood down from the upcoming series after the charge. Her statement said reports about her private life did not reflect events as she understood them; she said she would cooperate with authorities and could not comment further during the legal process. ITV accepted her decision.

evidence.label: Laura Whitmore named host, 20 December 2019
evidence.text: ITV announced Laura Whitmore as the replacement host after Flack stepped down; Whitmore described Flack as a friend and said she wished circumstances were better.

evidence.label: Not-guilty plea reported, 24 December 2019
evidence.text: ITV’s 24 December report states Flack pleaded not guilty at Highbury Corner Magistrates’ Court on 23 December. She remained on bail ahead of a trial then scheduled for March. The same report records her statement that scrutiny and speculation were difficult to face alone and that she was taking time away to feel better.

evidence.label: Reported headline of removed Sun online story
evidence.text: The Independent reported that The Sun published an online story on 14 February about a Valentine card mocking Flack in relation to the alleged assault; it reproduced the headline excerpt “Brutal Caroline Flack Valentine’s Day card mocks troubled star”. This confirms an online story, not its presence in the Guardian’s print corpus.

evidence.label: Removal reported after the window
evidence.text: By Saturday evening, 15 February, the online story had been replaced with a legal removal notice. The Guardian says the exact removal time was unclear, so the record does not establish whether removal preceded or followed the public announcement. This is outside the print-count window.

evidence.label: Public debate about press coverage
evidence.text: The Guardian reported criticism of tabloid coverage and recorded The Sun executive editor Dan Wootton’s public claim that ITV had failed to stand by Flack. The response and criticism are viewpoints, not evidence that coverage caused her death.

evidence.label: Public Strain
evidence.text: Reports her public response and stated distress after the hearing.

evidence.label: LBC report on Burton’s response to circulated bedroom photographs (1 January 2020)
evidence.text: This verified LBC headline reports that Burton denied the blood shown on a stained bed was his. It reports his response; it does not identify whose blood it was or independently establish the photographs’ origin.

evidence.label: Relationship Rumour
evidence.text: Reports Flack's objection to gossip coverage amid breakup reports.

evidence.label: Valentine Card
evidence.text: A new mocking-card item on 14 February; distinct from the 2019 alleged incident, though it echoes the lamp allegation.

evidence.label: Court Eve Distress
evidence.text: Reports a distinct pre-hearing statement, one day before the plea hearing.

briefing.title: A fictional desk defence of its sampled coverage

paragraphs.text: We would defend reporting distinct developments in this sample: the charge, Flack’s decision to step down, the replacement host, the plea, and her public response to gossip. These events had public interest because she was a high-profile presenter and the programme was imminent. Our nine retained records are clustered around those changes, not a complete archive.

We would distinguish the allegation from the not-guilty plea and from any later outcome. The charge was not a conviction, and no trial verdict occurred in this window. When Burton’s statements or relationship rumours were reported, we should attribute them and avoid presenting a denial as proof of every underlying claim.

We would say our role is to report verifiable public developments, not turn a private life into ongoing entertainment. Headlines about distress or gossip need particular care. We would ask whether a new item adds information or simply sustains attention after Flack had publicly objected to speculation.

This recovered set is incomplete and event-led. The separately reported print aggregate is not our daily series and cannot establish tone, intent, harm or cause. One later report reproduced a mocking online card headline; its original page is unavailable. Readers should be able to distinguish direct publisher records from reproduced wording.

briefing.title: A fictional desk defence of its sampled coverage

paragraphs.text: We would defend reporting the charge, Flack’s decision to step down, the replacement host, the court hearing and her Christmas message because each was a dated public development. Our six retained records also include a programme change with direct relevance to viewers and the production.

We would state the procedural facts carefully: the charge was an allegation; Flack pleaded not guilty; the hearing set a future trial. We would include her position and avoid repeating prosecution assertions as established fact. The plea did not resolve the case.

When Flack said scrutiny and speculation were difficult and she was taking a break from social media, we would recognize that as a signal to examine the value of further attention. Public interest in a presenter’s role does not make every detail of her private life newsworthy.

These six retained records are part of an incomplete sample across several outlets. Missing dates do not prove nothing else ran. A separate long-window print aggregate has no itemized daily series here. Counts can prompt questions about repetition and editorial choices, but they do not establish intent or causation.

briefing.title: A fictional desk defence of its sampled coverage

paragraphs.text: We would defend reporting the charge and its consequences for a prominent television programme, then covering the replacement host and court plea as further developments. Our sample has three retained headlines: the charge, the host appointment, and the not-guilty plea. It is an event-led selection, not a full archive. The dated sources let readers check each step.

We would keep the allegation and response distinct. Flack pleaded not guilty; neither the charge nor the plea was a verdict. Reports should identify the procedural status and avoid treating details alleged in court as findings.

As the story shifted to her public statements about distress and online gossip, care should shape prominence and repetition. We would ask whether a new item adds information or simply sustains attention to her private life. Later commentary should not be used to claim causation.

The separately reported count of 99 print stories mentioning Flack over a longer period is not a list of headlines or this sample. Recovered records are uneven, so any chart shows sample counts only. We would link sources, state what remains unknown, and invite readers to question proportionality.

briefing.title: A fictional desk defence of its sampled coverage

paragraphs.text: We would defend publication of the Valentine-card item as a dated online story about a public figure and a public court case. The prior allegation was relevant to understanding the card’s lamp reference, and the item reported a topical social-media response. Our sample contains one such record, not a measure of all our coverage.

A topical card and its circulation can be newsworthy, but that does not settle whether a mocking frame was fair. We would say the article reported a joke circulating around a high-profile case; critics can reasonably ask whether the presentation turned unresolved allegations into entertainment and whether the public gained useful information.

We would acknowledge the case had not been tried: Flack pleaded not guilty, so the accusation was unresolved. The exact original page is unavailable; the headline survives as wording reproduced in a later report. That report’s page has since changed to a removal story. We cannot imply the quotation is current page metadata.

This single recovered online item is outside the separate print-story aggregate and cannot establish its daily pace or tone. We would defend newsworthiness while accepting scrutiny of taste, care and proportionality. Neither the headline nor a count proves motive, harm or any cause of death.

publicContext.intro: Caroline Flack was a television presenter. After a criminal charge in December 2019, reports followed her court appearance, her departure from Love Island and her private life. She died in February 2020. This timeline ends before her death: you judge the reporting choices using the events and information available then.
publicContext.allegationResponse: The case does not establish what caused her death. The 99 Sun print-story figure covers a separate six-month analysis; it is not the number of headlines in this dated sample.
